identification.summary: Madi (also spelled Mahdi) is a cyber-espionage campaign disclosed in July 2012 by Kaspersky Lab and Seculert, who sinkholed its command-and-control servers and monitored it [S1]. Over roughly eight months they identified more than 800 victims, mostly in Iran and Israel, including people working on Iranian and Israeli critical-infrastructure projects, Israeli financial institutions, Middle Eastern engineering students and government bodies [S1]. The name comes from a file, mahdi.txt, dropped on infected machines [S2][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Seculert tracked variants of the same malware back to December 2011 [S4]. Public disclosure was 2012-07-17 [S1][S2].
identification.notes: Kaspersky uses 'Madi' and Seculert uses 'Mahdi' [S6]. This is a named campaign and malware family, not a vendor-tracked actor with a Microsoft name or MITRE group ID; no Microsoft name is assigned. Victim-distribution figures differ by dataset (see gaps).

attribution.confidence: No source gathered attributes Madi to a government. Seculert found Farsi strings and Persian-calendar dates in components, and its CTO said the author was fluent in Persian [S2][S4]. Symantec suggested an unknown Farsi-speaking individual with a broad agenda [S4]. Kaspersky and Seculert found no apparent connection to Flame and did not speculate on a sponsor [S4]. Seculert's CTO later said mounting evidence suggested the malware was built by Iranians, primarily to spy on people inside Iran [S3].
attribution.basis: Language artifacts (Farsi strings, Persian-calendar dates), victim set, and early C2 hosting in Tehran before servers moved to Canada, per Seculert as reported by press [S4][S3]. These are circumstantial vendor observations, not government attribution.

objectives: Surveillance of selected individuals and organizations: the malware stole files, logged keystrokes, captured screenshots and recorded audio [S1][S5]. Spied-on applications included Gmail, Hotmail, Yahoo! Mail, ICQ, Skype, Google+ and Facebook, plus ERP/CRM and financial systems [S1]. The sponsor's strategic intent is not established in the sources gathered.

sectors: Critical infrastructure project personnel (Iran and Israel)
regions: Later victims reported in the United States and Germany [S3]
targeting.notes: Sinkhole counts reported by press: at least 387 computers in Iran, 54 in Israel, 14 in Afghanistan, 6 in the UAE and 4 in Saudi Arabia [S6]. Symantec's data put about 72 percent of targets in Israel, a figure that may reflect Symantec's customer base [S5]. Seculert reported more than 150 new victims since June, including some tied to the US and Germany [S3].

capabilities.summary: Spread by rogue emails using basic social engineering, with specially crafted PowerPoint files; lures included a missile-test video and a copy of a Daily Beast article on Israel-Iran electronic warfare [S2][S5]. The Trojan stole files, logged keystrokes, took screenshots at set intervals, recorded audio and could update itself [S1][S5]. Kaspersky called the malware crude, yet the operators sustained surveillance [S2][S5]. A variant compiled 25 July 2012 added monitoring of Jabber and VKontakte conversations and uploaded stolen data to the server without waiting for commands [S6].

campaigns.name: Earliest known variants
campaigns.summary: Seculert traced variants of the malware to December 2011, when the C2 domain was hosted on a server in Tehran; main servers later moved to Canada.

campaigns.name: Continued victim growth
campaigns.summary: Seculert reported more than 150 new victims since June 2012, including some tied to the US and Germany. The first victim using a 'Flame' prefix began contacting C2 in early June; researchers found no apparent link to Flame.

campaigns.name: Public disclosure and sinkholing
campaigns.summary: Kaspersky Lab and Seculert announced Madi after sinkholing the C2 servers; more than 800 victims over about eight months, mostly in Iran and Israel. Symantec published its own analysis the next day.

campaigns.name: New variant after C2 takedown
campaigns.summary: A variant compiled 25 July added Jabber and VKontakte monitoring and immediate data upload, showing the operation continued after C2 domains were shut down.

campaigns.name: Follow-up reporting of continued infections
campaigns.summary: The Hacker News reported in September 2012 that Iran remained a target and infections continued.

diamond.adversary: Unknown, Persian-speaking developer(s); Farsi strings and Persian-calendar dates in code. No government attribution in the sources gathered [S2][S4].
diamond.capability: Email-delivered PowerPoint lures with a Trojan providing file theft, keylogging, screenshots, audio capture and self-update [S1][S5].
diamond.infrastructure: Four C2 servers sinkholed by Kaspersky and Seculert; early hosting in Tehran, later in Canada [S1][S4].
diamond.victim: Individuals and organizations in Iran and Israel tied to infrastructure projects, finance, engineering and government, plus smaller numbers elsewhere [S1][S6].
diamond.socioPolitical: Iran-Israel tension supplied the lure themes (missile test, electronic-warfare article) [S2][S5]. Sponsor motive is not established.
diamond.technology: Reliance on user opening of Office attachments and on commonly used webmail, messaging and business-application accounts that were monitored [S1][S5].

gaps: No sponsor is established. Language clues are circumstantial and do not identify a state actor [S2][S4].
Victim distribution conflicts: sinkhole data (Kaspersky/Seculert) pointed mostly to Iran, while Symantec reported about 72 percent in Israel; the cause is not resolved in the sources [S5].

The Securelist 'Madi Campaign' Parts I and II, the CFR Cyber Operations Tracker entry, the Symantec blog (archived) and Threatpost article listed in the record could not be opened in this session; technical detail here relies on press coverage.
Several press sources are cited at month-level dates because exact publication days were not visible.
No activity after late 2012 was found; whether the operators persisted or retooled is unknown.
Overlap with Flame was examined by researchers who found no apparent connection [S4]; no link to other named actors is established.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is the user endpoint and its webmail, messaging and ERP/CRM accounts, not hardened infrastructure [S1]. STEP 2: The adversary used a low-sophistication Trojan with topical lures and sustained collection, so persistence rather than technical novelty is the threat [S2][S5]. STEP 3: The template is a themed email with a PowerPoint attachment, then Trojan install, then keylogging, screenshots, audio and file theft to C2 [S5]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued low-cost surveillance of individuals tied to regional infrastructure, finance and government. MDCOA is retooled variants that add messaging platforms and rapid exfiltration, as the July 2012 variant did [S6]. Candidate indicators: unexpected PowerPoint attachments with geopolitical lures, mahdi.txt on hosts, and periodic outbound uploads from user workstations [S3][S5]. Relevance to US forces is indirect and historical; the sources show limited US victimization [S3].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: treat this as a historical regional-espionage case study; no current activity was found. (2) Authorities: sinkholing was done by private vendors, so any takedown of similar infrastructure needs legal review and partner coordination. (3) Mission assurance: protect planners' personal and commercial webmail and messaging accounts, which this campaign targeted [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with vendors and partners, noting that takedown did not end the campaign, since a new variant appeared after C2 domains were shut down [S6].

provenance.importedSummary: Kaspersky Lab and Seculert worked together to sinkhole the Madi Command & Control (C&C) servers to monitor the campaign. Kaspersky Lab and Seculert identified more than 800 victims located in Iran, Israel and select countries across the globe connecting to the C&Cs over the past eight months. Statistics from the sinkhole revealed that the victims were primarily business people working on Iranian and Israeli critical infrastructure projects, Israeli financial institutions, Middle Eastern engineering students, and various government agencies communicating in the Middle East. Common applications and websites that were spied on include accounts on Gmail, Hotmail, Yahoo! Mail, ICQ, Skype, Google+, and Facebook. Surveillance is also performed over integrated ERP/CRM systems, business contracts, and financial management systems.
